paragraphs: First of all, Alyosha went to his father. On the way he remembered that his father had insisted the day before that he should come without his brother Ivan seeing him. “Why so?” Alyosha suddenly wondered. “Even if my father has something to say to me alone, why should I go in unseen? Most likely he meant to say something different yesterday, in his excitement,” he decided. Still, he was very glad when Marfa Ignatyevna, who opened the garden gate to him (Grigory, it seemed, was ill in bed in the lodge), answered his question by telling him that Ivan Fyodorovitch had gone out two hours ago.
“And my father?”
“He’s up, having his coffee,” Marfa answered rather dryly.

Alyosha went in. The old man was sitting alone at the table in slippers and a little old overcoat. He was amusing himself by looking through some accounts, though rather absentmindedly. He was quite alone in the house, since Smerdyakov had gone out to the market too. He had got up early and was trying to put a bold face on it, but he looked tired and weak. His forehead, where huge purple bruises had come out during the night, was bandaged with a red handkerchief. His nose had swollen terribly in the night as well, and some smaller bruises covered it in patches, which gave his whole face a peculiarly spiteful, irritable look. The old man knew it, and he turned a hostile glance on Alyosha as he came in.
“The coffee’s cold,” he cried harshly. “I won’t offer you any. I’ve ordered nothing today but a Lenten fish soup, and I’m not inviting anyone to share it. Why have you come?”
“To find out how you are,” said Alyosha.
“Yes. Besides, I told you to come yesterday. It’s all of no consequence. You needn’t have bothered. But I knew you’d come poking in right away.”

He said this with almost hostile feeling. At the same time he got up and looked anxiously at his nose in the looking-glass (perhaps for the fortieth time that morning). He began, too, to tie his red handkerchief more becomingly on his forehead.
“Red’s better. A white one makes it look just like the hospital,” he observed solemnly. “Well, how are things over there? How is your elder?”
“He is very bad. He may die today,” answered Alyosha. But his father had not listened, and had already forgotten his own question.
“Ivan’s gone out,” he said suddenly. “He’s doing his utmost to carry off Mitya’s betrothed. That’s what he’s staying here for,” he added maliciously, and, twisting his mouth, looked at Alyosha.
“Surely he didn’t tell you so?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, he did, long ago. Would you believe it, he told me three weeks ago? You don’t suppose he came to murder me too, do you? He must have had some purpose in coming.”
“What do you mean? Why do you say such things?” said Alyosha, troubled.

“He doesn’t ask for money, it’s true, but he won’t get a farthing from me anyway. I intend to live as long as I can, you may as well know, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, and so I need every farthing, and the longer I live, the more I’ll need,” he went on, pacing from one corner of the room to the other, with his hands in the pockets of his loose, greasy overcoat made of yellow cotton. “I can still pass for a man of fifty-five, but I want to pass for one for another twenty years. As I get older, you know, I won’t be a pretty sight. The wenches won’t come to me of their own accord, so I’ll want my money. So I’m saving up more and more, just for myself, my dear son Alexey Fyodorovitch. You may as well know it. For I mean to go on in my sins to the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet. Everyone abuses it, but everyone lives in it, only the others do it on the sly and I do it openly. And so all the other sinners fall on me for being so simple. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, is not to my taste, let me tell you that. It’s not the proper place for a gentleman, your paradise, even if it exists. I believe that I fall asleep and don’t wake up again, and that’s all. You can pray for my soul if you like. And if you don’t want to, don’t, damn you! That’s my philosophy. Ivan talked well here yesterday, though we were all drunk. Ivan is a conceited coxcomb, but he has no particular learning ... no education either. He sits silent and smiles at you without speaking—that’s what pulls him through.”
Alyosha listened to him in silence.

“Why won’t he talk to me? If he does speak, he gives himself airs. Your Ivan is a scoundrel! And I’ll marry Grushenka in a minute if I want to. Because if you’ve got money, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you only have to want a thing and you can have it. That’s what Ivan’s afraid of. He’s on the watch to keep me from getting married, and that’s why he’s egging Mitya on to marry Grushenka himself. He hopes to keep me away from Grushenka that way (as though I’d leave him my money if I don’t marry her!). Besides, if Mitya marries Grushenka, Ivan will carry off his rich betrothed. That’s what he’s reckoning on! He’s a scoundrel, your Ivan!”
“How cross you are! It’s because of yesterday. You had better lie down,” said Alyosha.

“There! You say that,” the old man observed suddenly, as though it had only just struck him, “and I’m not angry with you. But if Ivan said it, I’d be angry with him. It’s only with you that I have good moments, otherwise, you know, I’m an ill-natured man.”
“You’re not ill-natured, just twisted,” said Alyosha with a smile.

“Listen. This morning I meant to have that ruffian Mitya locked up, and now I don’t know what I’ll decide. Of course, in these fashionable days fathers and mothers are looked on as a prejudice, but even now the law doesn’t allow you to drag your old father about by the hair, to kick him in the face in his own house, and to brag that you’ll murder him outright—all in front of witnesses. If I wanted to, I could crush him and have him locked up at once for what he did yesterday.”
“Then you don’t mean to take legal action?”
“Ivan has talked me out of it. I wouldn’t care about Ivan, but there’s another thing.”
And bending down to Alyosha, he went on in a confidential half-whisper.

“If I send the ruffian to prison, she’ll hear of it and run to see him at once. But if she hears that he beat me, a weak old man, within an inch of my life, she may give him up and come to me.... That’s her way, everything by contraries. I know her through and through! Won’t you have a drop of brandy? Take some cold coffee and I’ll pour a quarter of a glass of brandy into it. It’s delicious, my boy.”

“No, thank you. I’ll take that roll with me, if I may,” said Alyosha, and he took a halfpenny French roll and put it in the pocket of his cassock. “And you’d better not have brandy either,” he suggested anxiously, looking into the old man’s face.
“You’re quite right, it irritates my nerves instead of soothing them. Only one little glass. I’ll get it out of the cupboard.”
He unlocked the cupboard, poured out a glass and drank it, then locked the cupboard and put the key back in his pocket.
“That’s enough. One glass won’t kill me.”
“You see, you’re in a better mood now,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Hm! I love you even without the brandy, but with scoundrels I’m a scoundrel. Ivan isn’t going to Tchermashnya—why is that? He wants to spy on how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They’re all scoundrels! But I don’t recognize Ivan, I don’t know him at all. Where does he come from? He’s not one of us in his soul. As though I’d leave him anything! I won’t leave a will at all, you may as well know. And I’ll crush Mitya like a beetle. I squash black-beetles at night with my slipper. They squelch when you tread on them. And your Mitya will squelch too. _Your_ Mitya, because you love him. Yes, you love him, and I’m not afraid of your loving him. But if Ivan loved him I’d be afraid, for myself, at his loving him. But Ivan loves nobody. Ivan is not one of us. People like Ivan are not our sort, my boy. They’re like a cloud of dust. When the wind blows, the dust will be gone.... I had a silly idea in my head when I told you to come today. I wanted to find out from you about Mitya. If I were to hand him a thousand or maybe two now, would the beggarly wretch agree to take himself off altogether for five years or, better still, thirty-five, and without Grushenka, and give her up once and for all, eh?”
“I—I’ll ask him,” muttered Alyosha. “If you would give him three thousand, perhaps he—”

“That’s nonsense! You needn’t ask him now, no need! I’ve changed my mind. It was a nonsensical idea of mine. I won’t give him anything, not a penny, I want my money myself,” cried the old man, waving his hand. “I’ll crush him like a beetle without it. Don’t say anything to him, or else he’ll start hoping. There’s nothing for you to do here, you needn’t stay. Is that betrothed of his, Katerina Ivanovna, whom he’s kept so carefully hidden from me all this time, going to marry him or not? You went to see her yesterday, I believe?”
“Nothing will make her abandon him.”

“There, you see how dearly these fine young ladies love a rake and a scoundrel. They’re poor creatures, I tell you, those pale young ladies, very different from—Ah, if I had his youth and the looks I had then (because I was better-looking than he is, at twenty-eight) I’d have been a conquering hero just as he is. He’s a low cad! But he shan’t have Grushenka, anyway, he shan’t! I’ll crush him!”
His anger had come back with the last words.
“You can go. There’s nothing for you to do here today,” he snapped harshly.
Alyosha went up to say good-by to him, and kissed him on the shoulder.
“What’s that for?” The old man was a little surprised. “We’ll see each other again, or do you think we won’t?”
“Not at all, I didn’t mean anything.”

“Nor did I, I didn’t mean anything,” said the old man, looking at him. “Listen, listen,” he shouted after him, “come again soon and I’ll have a fish soup for you, a fine one, not like today’s. Be sure to come! Come tomorrow, do you hear, tomorrow!”
And as soon as Alyosha had gone out of the door, he went to the cupboard again and poured out another half-glass.

“I won’t have more!” he muttered, clearing his throat, and again he locked the cupboard and put the key in his pocket. Then he went into his bedroom and lay down on the bed, exhausted, and in a minute he was asleep.
